lesson.title: The Turning Point: Finding a Parabola's Vertex
lesson.summary: The vertex is the single point where a parabola changes direction, and standard form gives you a direct formula, x = -b/(2a), for locating it.
lesson.body:
Every parabola has exactly one point where it stops going one direction and starts going the other, the bottom of the bowl if it opens upward, or the top of the frown if it opens downward. That turning point is called the vertex. In the table you built for f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 in the last section, the vertex was visible directly: the y-values decreased down to -1 at x = 2, then increased again, so (2, -1) was the lowest point on the curve.

You do not have to build a whole table to find the vertex, though. For a quadratic in standard form, f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, the x-coordinate of the vertex is given by the formula x = -b / (2a). Once you have that x-value, find the corresponding y-value the same way you would evaluate the function at any other input: substitute it back into f(x).

Apply this to f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3. Here a = 1, b = -4, and c = 3. The vertex's x-coordinate is x = -b/(2a) = -(-4)/(2·1) = 4/2 = 2. To get the y-coordinate, substitute x = 2 back into the function: f(2) = (2)^2 - 4(2) + 3 = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1. So the vertex is (2, -1), exactly matching what the table of values showed in the previous section.

Since a = 1 is positive, this parabola opens upward, which means the vertex is the lowest point on the entire curve, the function never produces an output smaller than -1. If a had been negative, the same formula would still locate the vertex, but it would be the highest point instead. That distinction, and what the vertex's y-value actually represents for the function, is exactly what the next two sections, maximum value and minimum value, are about.
